docs.title: pixi-oci
docs.text:
A pixi extension that builds OCI container images straight from pixi.lock: no Dockerfile, no Docker or Podman, no daemon and no admin rights. The lockfile already names every package, its URL and its sha256; pixi-oci turns exactly those packages into an image that docker, podman, skopeo, crane and OpenShift all read.

pixi oci plan  -e app -p linux-64                       # the layers, without downloading anything
pixi oci build -e app -p linux-64 --tag app:1.0 -o app.tar
podman load -i app.tar                                  # or docker load, or skopeo copy oci-archive:app.tar ...

Early days

plan and build work today, for environments of conda packages, on Linux, macOS and Windows. Images have no base image yet, so a dynamically linked program (python, most of conda-forge) needs the glibc a base provides before it runs in a container. Base images and pushing to a registry are next: see the roadmap.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
The usual way to containerize a pixi environment is a multi-stage Dockerfile that installs pixi, runs pixi install, and copies the environment into a slimmer stage. That needs a Docker daemon or a privileged builder, downloads everything again on every cache miss, and produces layers that say nothing about which packages they hold.

pixi-oci builds from the lockfile instead:

  • Daemonless and rootless. It writes the image itself, on a laptop with no admin rights, a plain CI runner, or an OpenShift build pod.
  • Windows too. Layers are written straight from the package archives, so the host's file system never has to hold Linux modes or symlinks.
  • Reproducible. The same lockfile gives the same image digest on every machine; CI checks Linux, macOS and Windows against each other on every change.
  • Layers that cache well. Large packages get layers of their own and small ones share a few, dependencies at the bottom, so changing one package re-uploads one small layer, and images built from the same packages share layers in the registry.
  • Checked. Every archive must match the sha256 the lockfile recorded before anything reads it.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
pixi-oci is one Rust binary, organized as a short pipeline. Each stage has one module and one job.

 pixi.lock ─▶ lock.rs ─▶ plan.rs ─▶ build.rs ─┬─▶ fetch.rs ─▶ cache: archives/<sha256>.conda
                │           │          │      │
                │           │          │      └─▶ stream.rs ─▶ layer.rs ─▶ blobs/sha256/<digest>   (per layer, in parallel)
                │           │          │            ▲
                │           │          │            └── target.rs: the prefix, the platform, python
                │           │          └──────────▶ image.rs ─▶ config, manifest, index.json, .tar
                │           └─ platform.rs: conda platform to OCI platform
                └─ report.rs: a plan as text or JSON          cli.rs and lib.rs: the command line around it
Module Job cli.rs The command line (clap). pixi runs pixi-oci for pixi oci and passes everything after oci. lib.rs Runs a parsed command line and returns what to print. lock.rs Reads pixi.lock (rattler_lock) into the packages of one environment and platform, each with its URL, sha256, size, dependencies and repodata record. plan.rs Splits those packages into layers as --layers says: large packages alone and small ones grouped at cut points their names fix (the default), one per package, or one for everything; dependencies first with ties by name, capped by --max-layers, PyPI on top. platform.rs Maps linux-* conda platforms to OCI platforms (linux-aarch64 to linux/arm64/v8), and picks the default. report.rs A plan as a table or JSON. build.rs build: checks the request, fetches every archive, writes the planned layers in parallel within --max-memory, puts a pulled base's layers underneath, merges its config, then writes the image. fetch.rs Downloads conda archives (ureq), checks each against the lockfile's sha256, and keeps it in a cache named by that hash. stream.rs Writes one layer straight from its packages' archives: placeholder replacement, noarch: python placement and entry points, conda-meta records, the prefix guard, and the piecewise rewrite of large files. target.rs The install target: the prefix in the image, the platform, and python for noarch packages. layer.rs The layer writer: a GNU tar, gzip-compressed, every entry root-owned with one time and one of three modes, hashed twice on the way (diff_id and digest). image.rs The image config, manifest, OCI layout, docker-compatible manifest.json, and the .tar archive. check.rs check: the layers applied into a map of facts (modes, ELF dynamic sections, shebangs, placeholders), then the loader's and the shell's lookups run inside it. inspect.rs inspect: an image's settings and layers, with each layer's packages read from its history line. registry.rs A base image pulled from a registry, pinned by digest: the platform's manifest from an index, its config and layers, each checked against its digest and cached by it. Anonymous or with docker's and podman's credentials, through bearer tokens or basic auth. wheel.rs A PyPI wheel installed into a layer as pip and uv install one: site-packages, scripts, headers, data, entry point launchers, every file checked against the wheel's RECORD and a new RECORD written. read.rs An image read back: a layout directory, or a .tar read in place by each file's offset, never unpacked. validate.rs validate: every blob, digest, size, media type and diff_id of an image checked against the OCI image spec, with every problem collected.

docs.title: Decisions that shape the code
docs.text:
Nothing of a layer touches the host. stream.rs reads archive entries and writes them into the layer's tar directly; the only files a build writes are archives, blobs and spill files, all named by hashes. This is what makes builds work on Windows, and it keeps a crafted archive's member names from ever reaching the host's file system.

Install like rattler. stream.rs follows rattler::install::link_package_sync step for step and uses rattler's public functions where they exist (placeholder replacement, noarch paths, the entry-point template, PrefixRecord). install.rs keeps rattler's own linker as a test-only reference, and parity.rs holds the two to the same output.

Reproducible bytes. Anything that would bring a time, a host path, a user name or an unordered collection into a layer or the config would change image digests. Entries keep the archives' order, modes are normalized, times come from SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, and the gzip header is empty.

Bounded memory. A file is held whole only up to the in-memory limit; larger rewrites go through a temporary file in pieces cut where no replacement can cross. build::budget turns --max-memory into that limit and a number of parallel layers.

One rattler release set. rattler, rattler_conda_types, rattler_lock, rattler_package_streaming and rattler_digest are pinned exactly to one set, because they pin each other exactly; they move together.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Where What Unit tests in each module the module's own rules: planning, platforms, tar determinism, the budget, cut points, errors src/parity.rs (Unix) every test plan built the streamed way and through rattler's linker, file for file; generated packages always, conda-forge's with PIXI_OCI_NETWORK_TESTS=1 src/testing.rs conda packages made in tests (both archive formats, placeholders, symlinks, noarch python), images read back tests/cli.rs the binary end to end against tests/fixtures/workspace/pixi.lock tests/network.rs (Linux, PIXI_OCI_NETWORK_TESTS=1) a real image from conda-forge, unpacked, and its python run CI's Image digest jobs the fixture image built on Linux, macOS and Windows; one digest required

docs.title: Base images
docs.text:
conda packages bring almost everything a program needs, but not the C library: conda-forge builds against the system's glibc and expects the image to have one, along with its loader (/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2) and usually /bin/sh and /usr/bin/env for scripts. An image built without a base has none of these, which is why pixi oci check reports a glibc problem for it.

--base builds the environment on an image that has them:

pixi oci build --base registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal@sha256:baafce2d34783a28b4a472779f304e97e00f9d35c99553bc53b068b14344d9a9 \
  --entrypoint python -o app.tar

Any image works, from any registry. These two are the ones the project documents and tests in CI, built on and run for linux-64 and linux-aarch64:

Red Hat UBI 9 minimal Debian 12 slim Image registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal debian:bookworm-slim glibc 2.34 2.36 Shell, env yes yes Package manager microdnf apt Perl no perl-base Size, compressed about 38 MiB about 28 MiB Pinned in CI sha256:baafce2d34783a28b4a472779f304e97e00f9d35c99553bc53b068b14344d9a9 sha256:734a72b3d6142a71993b4bc580ca01d8ca687f77a2c422d96a961d3376b179bc

UBI images are freely redistributable and supported by Red Hat, which suits places where RHEL and OpenShift are the standard; Debian slim is the common base for Python images. Both have a newer glibc than conda-forge needs (2.17, or 2.28 for its newer builds). Smaller bases work too: ubi9/ubi-micro (no package manager) or gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian12 (no shell, so check will name the scripts that need one).

docs.title: Pinned by digest
docs.text:
A base is always given with its digest, so the same lockfile and the same base build the same image, today and in a year. A tag alone is refused. Find a tag's digest with any of:

crane digest debian:bookworm-slim
skopeo inspect docker://debian:bookworm-slim --format '{{.Digest}}'
docker buildx imagetools inspect debian:bookworm-slim

The digest can be an index's, covering several platforms, or one platform's manifest. pixi-oci follows an index to the manifest for the platform being built, and refuses a base that has none for it.

docs.title: What the image gets from the base
docs.text:
The base's layers go first, as they were pulled, and the environment's on top. The config starts from the base's, as a Dockerfile's FROM does:

In the image PATH the environment's bin, then the base's PATH other variables the base's, with any that pixi-oci sets (CONDA_PREFIX, --env) replacing the base's of the same name entrypoint and command --entrypoint drops the base's command; --cmd alone keeps the base's entrypoint; neither keeps both working directory --workdir, else the base's user, ports, stop signal the base's labels the base's, then dev.pixi.environment, dev.pixi.platform and dev.pixi.base (the base's reference) history the base's, then a line per environment layer

The manifest records the base with the image spec's own annotations, org.opencontainers.image.base.name and org.opencontainers.image.base.digest. The base's layers count toward --max-layers.

docs.title: Registries and credentials
docs.text:
Bases are pulled over the registry API with no Docker or Podman, anonymously when the registry allows it. For a private registry, pixi-oci uses the credentials docker login and podman login keep, in this order: REGISTRY_AUTH_FILE, podman's auth.json, then docker's config.json, including its credential helpers (credHelpers, credsStore). Proxies come from HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY.

Every manifest, config and layer is checked against its digest and kept in the cache (--cache-dir) under blobs/sha256, so a base is downloaded once.

docs.title: Command-line reference
docs.text: pixi runs pixi-oci for pixi oci, passing everything after oci, so pixi oci build -e app and pixi-oci build -e app are the same command.

docs.title: pixi oci plan
docs.text:
Shows the layers an image of an environment would be built from, without downloading anything.

Option Default --lockfile PATH pixi.lock the lockfile to read -e, --environment NAME default the environment to put in the image -p, --platform NAME Linux on the host's architecture a linux-* conda platform: linux-64, linux-aarch64, linux-ppc64le, ... --layers grouped\|per-package\|single grouped how to split the environment into layers: packages of 4 MiB or more alone and smaller ones grouped, a layer per package, or the whole environment in one layer. See Planning the layers. --max-layers N 100 the most layers to use; past it, the layers of the packages fewest others depend on are merged into the last conda layer. At least 2, except with --layers single. --packages list the packages of every layer that holds several --format text\|json text json carries every package's kind, URL, sha256 and size

The default platform is linux-aarch64 on an ARM machine (an Apple Silicon Mac, an ARM server) and linux-64 everywhere else.

docs.title: pixi oci build
docs.text:
Builds an image of an environment. It takes plan's --lockfile, -e, -p, --layers and --max-layers, and:

Option Default -o, --output PATH image.tar a .tar archive, for docker load, podman load and skopeo copy oci-archive:; any other path is an OCI image layout directory --force replace the output if it exists -t, --tag NAME[:TAG] the environment's name, :latest the image's name: lowercase, optionally with a registry (quay.io/team/app:1.0) --prefix PATH /opt/env where the environment lives in the image; an absolute path --env KEY=VALUE an environment variable in the image; repeat for more --entrypoint COMMAND the entrypoint: a JSON array ('["python", "-m", "http.server"]') or words (python -m http.server) --cmd ARGS the default arguments, in the same two forms --workdir PATH the working directory processes start in --base IMAGE@DIGEST an image to build on, pinned by digest, for glibc and a shell: its layers go under the environment's and its config is where the image's starts (Base images) --max-memory SIZE 512M roughly how much memory the build's buffers may use, such as 128M or 2G; at least 16M. Less means fewer layers at once and large files waiting on disk; the image is the same. --cache-dir PATH see below where downloaded package archives are kept, named by their sha256

The image always sets PATH=<prefix>/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin and CONDA_PREFIX=<prefix>; --env adds to them. It is labelled dev.pixi.environment and dev.pixi.platform.

Progress goes to stderr, one line per layer as it starts. The summary goes to stdout:

Wrote app:1.0 to app.tar
  manifest sha256:9ec8407e4f1860919cd8dd7af6027a9bdcb91a5a008b2c5ea657ed3f300044ef
  7 layers, 62.6 MiB for linux/amd64

docs.title: pixi oci validate
docs.text:
Checks an image against the OCI image spec, on any OS, running nothing.

$ pixi oci validate app.tar
app.tar is a valid OCI image
  manifest sha256:9ec8407e4f18 for linux/amd64: 7 layers, 62.6 MiB
Argument or option Default IMAGE an OCI image layout directory, or a .tar archive of one, read in place --format text\|json text json gives valid, each manifest checked, and each problem as at and message

It checks:

  • oci-layout and index.json, and any index nested in it
  • every manifest and config: schema version, media types, and that the index lists each with its own media type
  • every blob: present, and its sha256 and size the ones its descriptor names
  • every layer: a layer media type, and for gzip and uncompressed layers, that its uncompressed tar hashes to the config's diff_id for it
  • the config: as many diff_ids and history entries as layers, and the same platform as the index
  • org.opencontainers.image.ref.name, by the spec's grammar
  • for an archive, that the manifest.json docker load reads names the same config and layers

It reports every problem it finds, not just the first, and exits 1 if there is any. zstd layers are hashed but their diff_id is not checked.

The image is a standard OCI image, so other tools check it the same way: crane validate --tarball app.tar, or skopeo copy oci-archive:app.tar ... as a smoke test.

docs.title: pixi oci check
docs.text:
Checks that an image will run, by Linux's rules, without running it, so it works on Windows and macOS too. It runs validate first, and looks at the files only if the image is valid.

$ pixi oci check app.tar
app.tar: 4 problems in 5195 files (134 ELF files, 56 scripts)
  glibc: glibc is not in the image: 129 ELF files need /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, libc.so.6, libdl.so.2, libm.so.6, libpthread.so.0, librt.so.1, libutil.so.1
    /opt/env/bin/bunzip2, /opt/env/bin/bzcat, /opt/env/bin/bzip2, and 126 more
    help: conda packages use the system's glibc: build on a base image that has it (`--base`, #12), or add the loader and libraries in a layer below the environment
  library: libX11.so.6 is needed by 1 ELF file, but the loader would not find it
    /opt/env/lib/libtk8.6.so
  shebang: 20 scripts start with #!/bin/sh, which is not in the image
    /opt/env/bin/bzdiff, /opt/env/bin/bzgrep, /opt/env/bin/bzmore, and 17 more
  ...
  note: entrypoint: the image sets no entrypoint or cmd, so a container needs a command
Argument or option Default IMAGE an OCI image layout directory, or a .tar archive of one, read in place -p, --platform NAME the only one for an image of several platforms, which one: linux/arm64/v8, or linux-aarch64 --format text\|json text json gives ok, what was checked, and each problem and note with every path it affects

It applies the layers in order, whiteouts included, and then:

Problem What it means architecture an ELF file is for another machine than the image's platform glibc ELF files need a loader or glibc libraries no layer provides: an image without a base has none library a library an ELF file needs (DT_NEEDED) is not where the loader would look: its RPATH or RUNPATH (with $ORIGIN), the image's LD_LIBRARY_PATH, then /lib, /usr/lib, /lib64, /usr/lib64 and the multiarch directories shebang an executable script's #! interpreter is not in the image; for #!/usr/bin/env prog, prog is looked for on the image's PATH placeholder a file still holds a conda build placeholder, so it was not rewritten for the image's prefix (conda-meta records and __pycache__ caches excepted) entrypoint the entrypoint, or cmd when there is none, is not on the image's PATH, or is not executable elf a file starts like an ELF file but cannot be read as one spec validate found a problem; the files were not looked at

Symlinks are followed as the kernel follows them. It exits 1 if there is any problem; a note, such as an image with no entrypoint, does not fail it. ELF files are parsed in memory up to 64 MiB, and from a temporary file beyond.

docs.title: pixi oci inspect
docs.text:
Shows what an image holds, read from its index, manifest and config, without opening a layer or needing skopeo or crane.

$ pixi oci inspect app.tar
Image app:1.0 (app.tar)
  platform    linux/amd64
  manifest    sha256:9ec8407e4f1860919cd8dd7af6027a9bdcb91a5a008b2c5ea657ed3f300044ef
  config      sha256:6ca92a53b6bf0bf0fc05e09b3e22b662af269f9136ff892344073894a1ad1312
  created     1970-01-01T00:00:00Z
  env         PATH=/opt/env/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
              CONDA_PREFIX=/opt/env
  labels      dev.pixi.environment=app
              dev.pixi.platform=linux-64

7 layers, 62.6 MiB

  #  Layer              Size      Digest
  1  4 packages         2.1 MiB   sha256:960cbb64893f
  2  libpython 3.13.18  13.9 MiB  sha256:12f0c952f0ec
  3  12 packages        8.3 MiB   sha256:cbef1ccd8e85
  4  tk 8.6.13          4.0 MiB   sha256:74ddf65a7bef
  5  3 packages         1.7 MiB   sha256:a8fb83f0c699
  6  python 3.13.18     32.6 MiB  sha256:a6cd4f82fa1e
  7  six 1.17.0         11.5 KiB  sha256:f0d9c9d4dea1
Argument or option Default IMAGE an OCI image layout directory, or a .tar archive of one, read in place -p, --platform NAME the only one for an image of several platforms, which one: linux/arm64/v8, or the conda name linux-aarch64 --packages list the packages of every layer that holds several --format text\|json text json gives every field, and each layer's digest, size, media type, diff_id, history line and packages --raw index\|manifest\|config print that stored document exactly, instead of the summary; its sha256 is its digest

Layer sizes are the compressed sizes the registry stores. The packages of each layer come from the history line pixi-oci writes for it; a layer another tool built shows its own history line instead.

Other OCI tools read the same image: skopeo inspect oci-archive:app.tar, skopeo inspect --config oci-archive:app.tar, or crane config and crane manifest on a pushed image.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable PIXI_OCI_CACHE_DIR the package cache, when --cache-dir is not given. Otherwise $XDG_CACHE_HOME/pixi-oci, ~/.cache/pixi-oci on Linux, ~/Library/Caches/pixi-oci on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\pixi-oci on Windows SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH seconds since the Unix epoch, stamped on every file and on the image's created time; 0 when unset. The reproducible-builds convention. HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY, NO_PROXY the proxy for downloads PIXI_OCI_NETWORK_TESTS for development only: 1 adds the tests that download from conda-forge

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code 0 success 1 the command failed, or validate found a problem; the message says why and usually what to do (Troubleshooting) 2 the command line was wrong: an unknown option or a value that does not parse

docs.title: Development guide
docs.text: This page is how the code is built, checked, tested and documented. For what the code does, see the architecture page.

docs.title: Toolchain
docs.text:
Everything runs through pixi. pixi.toml pins the Rust toolchain from conda-forge and defines every task; Cargo.toml describes the crate. You do not need rustup or a system Rust.

git clone https://github.com/millsks/pixi-oci
cd pixi-oci
pixi install          # rust, cargo-llvm-cov, pre-commit, taplo, typos, actionlint, ...
pixi run bootstrap    # installs the git pre-commit and commit-msg hooks
Task Runs Purpose fmt cargo fmt Format (rustfmt.toml: edition 2024, 120 columns) lint cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings Lint; warnings are errors check cargo check --all-targets Type-check without building test cargo test Unit, parity and end-to-end tests cov cargo llvm-cov --all-targets --fail-under-lines 90 Full suite with a 90% line-coverage gate build cargo build --release Optimized binary at target/release/pixi-oci pre-commit-run pre-commit run --all-files All hooks over the tree ci pre-commit-run → build → check → lint → cov The gate; must pass before work is done fixture pixi lock in tests/fixtures/workspace Re-lock the test fixture; never edit its lockfile by hand bootstrap pre-commit install ... One-time hook installation deny (lint environment) cargo deny check Advisories, licenses, banned crates and sources, against deny.toml msrv-check (msrv environment) cargo check --all-targets --locked Builds on the minimum supported Rust (1.95) docs-serve (docs environment) mkdocs serve Live preview of this site at http://127.0.0.1:8000 docs-build (docs environment) mkdocs build --strict Build the site into site/; a broken link or a page missing from the nav fails

docs.title: Tests that use the network
docs.text: PIXI_OCI_NETWORK_TESTS=1 pixi run test adds two tests that download from conda-forge: the parity test on real packages, and tests/network.rs, which builds an image, unpacks its layers and runs its python (Linux only). CI's Linux test job sets the variable. PIXI_OCI_CACHE_DIR keeps their downloads between runs.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
• A feature branch and a pull request for every change. Work is done when the PR's checks pass; CI result is the one check branch protection requires.
  • Conventional commit messages, which the commit-msg hook enforces.
  • When rattler changes how it installs, the parity tests fail first. Match rattler in stream.rs rather than changing the tests.

docs.title: CI
docs.text: Job What it proves Lint pre-commit, rustfmt, clippy and cargo check are clean Test (Linux, macOS, Windows) the suite passes on each; on Linux with the network tests Coverage gate at least 90% of lines are covered Dependency advisories and licenses cargo-deny is clean Builds on the MSRV the crate builds on Rust 1.95 Image digest (Linux, macOS, Windows), Same image on every host the fixture image has one digest on every host; the release binaries are kept as artifacts Docs this site builds strictly CI result every job above passed

docs.title: The documentation site
docs.text:
The site is MkDocs with the Material theme, configured in mkdocs.yml; its colours and heading font are in docs/overrides/pixi-oci.css. The pages are the Markdown files in docs/, plus SECURITY.md, which mkdocs_hooks.py publishes as the security page at build time from extra.repo_pages. The docs pixi environment is separate from the Rust one, so pixi run -e docs docs-serve does not pull in a Rust toolchain.

The Docs site workflow publishes the site to GitHub Pages, versioned with mike as pixi-sbom's is: a push to main that touches the docs deploys dev, a published release deploys its version (v0.2.0) and moves latest to it, and the site root opens latest, or dev before the first release. GitHub Pages must be set to deploy from GitHub Actions (Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source).

docs.title: Your first image
docs.text: This walks from a pixi.toml to an image you can inspect and load. It works the same on Linux, macOS and Windows.

docs.title: 1. A workspace
docs.text:
An image is built from one environment of a lockfile, for one Linux platform. Any pixi workspace works, as long as it locks a linux-* platform:

pixi.toml
[workspace]
name = "hello"
channels = ["conda-forge"]
platforms = ["linux-64", "linux-aarch64", "win-64", "osx-arm64"]

[dependencies]
python = "3.13.*"
six = "*"

pixi lock

Your own platform can stay in the list; only the linux-* ones can become images. PyPI dependencies work too, as long as pixi locks wheels for them.

docs.title: 2. Plan it
docs.text:
plan reads the lockfile and shows the layers, without downloading anything:

$ pixi oci plan -p linux-64
Environment default on linux-64 (image platform linux/amd64)
23 conda packages, 0 PyPI packages, 7 layers, 44.9 MiB to download
4 conda packages in layers of their own, 19 sharing 3 layers

  #  Layer              Download
  1  4 conda packages   1.8 MiB
  2  libpython 3.13.18  9.3 MiB
  3  12 conda packages  5.9 MiB
  4  tk 8.6.13          3.4 MiB
  5  3 conda packages   1.4 MiB
  6  python 3.13.18     23.2 MiB
  7  six 1.17.0         18.0 KiB

Packages of 4 MiB or more get a layer of their own, smaller ones share a few, and the ones everything depends on come first. --packages lists what each shared layer holds, and --format json gives the same plan with every package's URL, sha256 and size.

docs.title: 3. Build it
docs.text:
$ pixi oci build -p linux-64 --tag hello:1.0 -o hello.tar
[1/7] 4 conda packages (1.8 MiB)
...
[7/7] six 1.17.0 (18.0 KiB)
Wrote hello:1.0 to hello.tar
  manifest sha256:9ec8407e4f1860919cd8dd7af6027a9bdcb91a5a008b2c5ea657ed3f300044ef
  7 layers, 62.6 MiB for linux/amd64

Each package is downloaded once into the cache, checked against the lockfile's sha256, and written into its layer with its paths rewritten for /opt/env, where the environment lives in the image. Build again and you get the same manifest digest, on this machine or any other. (Your digest will differ from this one: it depends on exactly what your lockfile locks.)

The layers come to more than the download: conda packages are compressed with zstd, and OCI layers with gzip, which every container tool can read.

The output is a .tar archive here. Give -o a path that does not end in .tar (-o hello-image) for an OCI image layout directory instead.

That image holds the environment alone. conda packages use the system's glibc, so to run one, build it on a base image that has glibc and a shell, pinned by its digest (Base images):

pixi oci build -p linux-64 --tag hello:1.0 -o hello.tar --entrypoint python \
  --base registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal@sha256:baafce2d34783a28b4a472779f304e97e00f9d35c99553bc53b068b14344d9a9

debian:bookworm-slim@sha256:734a72b3d6142a71993b4bc580ca01d8ca687f77a2c422d96a961d3376b179bc works the same way.

docs.title: 4. Look inside
docs.text:
Check it against the OCI image spec, with nothing else installed:

$ pixi oci validate hello.tar
hello.tar is a valid OCI image
  manifest sha256:9ec8407e4f18 for linux/amd64: 7 layers, 62.6 MiB

See what is in it, and which packages each layer holds:

pixi oci inspect hello.tar              # platform, settings, and a row per layer
pixi oci inspect hello.tar --packages   # every package of every shared layer
pixi oci inspect hello.tar --raw config # the full image config, exactly as stored

Check that it would run, without running it:

pixi oci check hello.tar

It reads every binary and script. Built without a base, the image gets a glibc problem: nothing in it provides the loader every conda binary needs. Built with --base, it reports only what the environment itself lacks, if anything.

It is a standard OCI image, so any OCI tool reads it as well, with no daemon:

skopeo inspect oci-archive:hello.tar            # platform, layers, environment variables
skopeo inspect --config oci-archive:hello.tar   # the full image config
crane validate --tarball hello.tar              # every digest checked

The image sets PATH to /opt/env/bin:... and CONDA_PREFIX to /opt/env. Add your own settings with --env, --entrypoint, --cmd and --workdir (reference).

docs.title: 5. Load it
docs.text:
podman load -i hello.tar
docker load -i hello.tar

It does not run yet

The image holds the environment and nothing else: no base, so no glibc. docker run hello:1.0 python fails with exec /opt/env/bin/python: no such file or directory, which is the missing system loader. Base images (--base) are the next milestone on the roadmap; until then the image is for inspecting, scanning, and copying the environment onto a base of your own.

docs.title: Other platforms
docs.text:
Build for ARM servers from any machine, with no emulation, since nothing is run:

pixi oci build -p linux-aarch64 --tag hello:1.0-arm64 -o hello-arm64.tar

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
pixi.lock ─▶ plan ─▶ fetch ─▶ stream each archive ─▶ tar ─▶ gzip ─▶ blob    (one per layer, several at once)
                       │       rewrite paths, place                         │
                       │       noarch python, add                           ▼
                cache of archives   conda-meta            config ─▶ manifest ─▶ OCI layout, or a .tar of it
                named by sha256

docs.title: Planning the layers
docs.text:
plan reads one environment of pixi.lock for one platform and decides the layers:

  1. Large packages alone, small ones grouped. Layers are named by their sha256, so a change to one package re-uploads only the layer that holds it, and images built from the same packages share layers in the registry. A conda package of 4 MiB or more gets a layer of its own: those are the ones worth re-uploading alone. Smaller ones are grouped, from about 1 MiB to 8 MiB a group, so a few hundred packages do not each spend a layer on a few kilobytes. A group ends after a package whose name hashes to a cut point (about one name in four) once it holds 1 MiB, or at 8 MiB whatever the names. Because the cut points belong to names, not positions, adding or removing a package changes only the group it lands in, and the layers above keep their digests. A group still under 1 MiB when a large package comes along stays open past it, rather than become a tiny layer of its own.
  2. Dependencies first. The packages everything rests on (libgcc, openssl, python) sit at the bottom, where they change least often. Ties go by name, so the order is the same on every run; a dependency cycle (python and pip) is broken at its alphabetically first package.
  3. Capped. Overlay file systems limit the layer count (Docker's overlay2 refuses an image of more than about 128), so past --max-layers (100) the layers at the top of the order, the ones fewest others depend on, are merged into the last conda layer. Grouping keeps even a few hundred packages well under it: a 385-package data-science and Jupyter environment plans into 84 layers.
  4. PyPI on top. All PyPI packages share the top layer: they install into one site-packages and are usually what changes most.

--layers chooses another layout: per-package gives every conda package a layer of its own, as long as the cap allows, and single puts the whole environment, conda and PyPI, in one layer, which suits an image built once and never updated. plan --packages lists what each shared layer holds.

Conda packages pixi builds from source have no archive yet, so an environment with them is refused, by name; so are PyPI packages that are not wheels (sdists, git and path checkouts), which would have to be built.

docs.title: Fetching
docs.text: Every archive of the plan is fetched before any layer is written, one at a time, so a failed download stops the build early. Each is checked against the sha256 the lockfile recorded, and kept in the cache named by that hash. A file whose bytes are not the ones locked never reaches the cache, and two lockfiles that lock the same file share it. Local archives (a file:// URL or a path) are read where they are, and still checked.

docs.title: Writing a layer from the archives
docs.text:
A layer is written straight from its packages' archives, never unpacked on the host. For each package, its info/index.json, info/paths.json and (for noarch: python) info/link.json are read first, then its content is streamed in the archive's own order: the pkg-*.tar.zst inside a .conda, or the whole .tar.bz2. Only what paths.json lists is installed.

Each entry is placed as rattler, pixi's own installer, would place it, under the image's prefix (/opt/env):

Entry In the layer A file with no placeholder copied into the tar in 64 KiB chunks A file with the build-time placeholder prefix rewritten for the image's prefix with rattler's own replacement functions, text or binary as paths.json says A symlink the archive's link target, as is An empty directory a directory entry A noarch: python file moved from site-packages/ to lib/python3.X/site-packages/, and python-scripts/ to bin/

After the content come the package's entry-point scripts (for noarch: python) and its conda-meta/<name>.json record, built the way rattler builds it; the bottom layer also carries the environment's empty conda-meta/history. Where two packages in one layer install the same path, the later one wins, as it would installing one after the other.

A package that would place a file outside the prefix (a path with .., a root or a drive) is refused before any of its layer is written.

docs.title: Checked against rattler
docs.text: The test suite keeps rattler's own installer as a reference: it installs every test plan into a directory with rattler::install::link_package_sync, builds the same plan the streamed way, and requires the same files, modes, symlink targets and conda-meta records. It does so for generated packages that cover text and binary placeholders, symlinks, case-only names, both archive formats, entry points and very large files, and for real conda-forge environments. A numpy, pandas, scipy and scikit-learn environment matches too: 15,888 entries, none different.

docs.title: Installing PyPI wheels
docs.text:
A wheel is a zip archive, read in place and written into the layer as pip and uv install one into a conda environment's python:

In the wheel In the image its root, .data/purelib, .data/platlib lib/pythonX.Y/site-packages .data/scripts bin, executable, with a #!python first line pointed at the environment's python .data/headers include/pythonX.Y/<name> .data/data the prefix console_scripts and gui_scripts entry points a launcher each in bin, as pip writes them

Every file is checked against the wheel's own RECORD as it is written, and every path must stay inside the prefix. The installed RECORD lists where each file went, relative to site-packages, and INSTALLER says pixi-oci. Where a wheel installs a path a conda package of the same layer also installs, the wheel's file wins, as it would installing the wheels after the conda packages. Bytecode is not compiled into the image; python writes it on first import where it can. CI installs the same lockfile with pixi install and checks that site-packages holds the same files with the same bytes.

docs.title: Reproducible bytes
docs.text:
The same lockfile gives the same image digest on any machine:

  • every entry is owned by root (uid and gid 0) and stamped with one time: SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, or 0
  • every mode is 0755 (directories, symlinks, executables) or 0644: only whether a file is executable is kept, so no umask reaches the image
  • entries keep the archives' order, which the lockfile's hashes fix
  • the gzip header carries no time and no file name
  • the config's created time is the same SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH

Layers are tar archives in GNU format, compressed with gzip, so every container runtime and registry reads them. CI builds a test image on Linux, macOS and Windows on every change and fails if the digests differ; pixi oci validate, crane validate, umoci unpack and skopeo copy all accept the result.

docs.title: Memory and disk
docs.text:
"In memory" means one entry at a time, not the whole image. Entries flow from the archive through the tar and gzip writers to a blob on disk:

  • A file without the placeholder passes through in 64 KiB chunks, however large.
  • A file with the placeholder is held whole while it is rewritten, up to a limit: an eighth of --max-memory, between 1 and 16 MiB.
  • A larger one is copied to a temporary file and rewritten in pieces of up to 4 MiB, each cut where no replacement can cross: right after a NUL byte in a binary file (a placeholder sits in a C string, which a NUL ends), right after a newline in a text file (but not before a line starting #!). The bytes are the same as a whole-file rewrite, and the tests check it.

--max-memory (512M by default) also sets how many layers are written at once: as many as fit, allowing for the in-memory limit twice per layer and about 16 MiB of decompression and compression buffers, and no more than the machine has cores. It never changes the image.

Measured with a warm cache on 2 cores:

linux-64 image Packages Unpacked Time Peak memory python and six 23 317 MiB 2.9 s 48 MiB; 28 MiB with --max-memory 16M python, numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn 39 460 MiB 5.3 s 45 MiB

On disk, plan for the cache (the compressed archives, about the size of the download), the output (the layers, somewhat larger, since gzip compresses less than conda's zstd), and while a .tar is assembled, the layers twice.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pixi-oci is one executable, pixi-oci (pixi-oci.exe on Windows). pixi runs any pixi-<name> executable it finds as pixi <name>, so once pixi-oci is on your PATH, pixi oci works.

No release yet

pixi-oci has not been released, so there is no pixi global install pixi-oci yet. Packaging it on conda-forge is on the roadmap. Until then, build it from source, or take a binary from a CI run.

docs.title: A binary from CI
docs.text:
Every CI run on main and on pull requests builds release binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows in the Image digest jobs and keeps them as artifacts for a few days:

  1. Open the repository's Actions tab, then a recent CI run on main.
  2. Under Artifacts, download pixi-oci-ubuntu-latest, pixi-oci-macos-latest or pixi-oci-windows-latest.
  3. Unzip it and put pixi-oci (or pixi-oci.exe) in a folder on your PATH.

On Windows, a folder you own on your PATH needs no admin rights: pixi's own %USERPROFILE%\.pixi\bin works if pixi is installed, or add a folder to your user PATH under Edit environment variables for your account.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
Everything builds through pixi, which brings its own Rust toolchain from conda-forge:

git clone https://github.com/millsks/pixi-oci
cd pixi-oci
pixi run build                        # target/release/pixi-oci
cp target/release/pixi-oci ~/.local/bin/   # any folder on your PATH

Building from source on Windows

Rust on Windows links with Microsoft's C++ build tools, which usually take an administrator to install. Without them, use a binary from CI instead: running pixi-oci needs nothing installed.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
pixi oci --version
pixi oci --help

If pixi oci says the command is unknown, pixi cannot see the executable: run pixi-oci --version directly, and if that works, the folder it is in is not on the PATH pixi sees.

docs.title: What it needs at run time
docs.text:
• The network, to the channels your lockfile names (conda-forge, prefix.dev, a private channel), for the packages that are not in the cache yet. Proxies come from the usual HTTPS_PROXY / HTTP_PROXY / NO_PROXY variables.
  • Disk for the cache of package archives (about the size of the image) and the image itself. See Memory and disk.
  • Nothing else: no Docker, Podman, pixi, Python or admin rights. pixi is only needed to run it as pixi oci; pixi-oci works on its own.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
The aim: build anywhere, check anywhere, run in CI. A developer on a Windows laptop with no admin rights builds and checks an image; CI proves the very same image runs, because the digest matches across hosts.

Each item has an issue labelled roadmap, where its scope and acceptance criteria live and its pull requests are linked. Comment there before starting on one.

docs.title: Done
docs.text:
• [x] plan: read pixi.lock, map conda platforms to OCI platforms, order layers dependencies first, cap them (#6)
  • [x] build: download and verify packages against the lockfile's sha256, rewrite paths for the image's prefix, and write a reproducible OCI image layout or archive (#7)
  • [x] Streamed layers: written straight from the archives, so builds run on Windows and macOS file systems, with memory bounded by --max-memory; checked against rattler's own installer file for file (#8)
  • [x] Documentation: this site, versioned and published from main (#9)
  • [x] Grouped layers: packages of 4 MiB or more alone and small ones grouped at cut points their names fix, so a large environment keeps its layers for the packages worth re-uploading; --layers per-package and single too (#10)
  • [x] validate: an image checked against the OCI image spec on any OS, every blob, digest, size and diff_id (#25)
  • [x] inspect: an image's settings and layers, with the packages each layer holds, as text, JSON or the exact stored documents (#24)
  • [x] check: whether an image will run, without running it, on any OS: architecture, loader and glibc, libraries by the loader's own search, shebangs, placeholders, the entrypoint (#11)
  • [x] Base images: --base builds on any image pinned by digest, pulled from any registry with docker's and podman's credentials; UBI 9 minimal and Debian 12 slim documented and run in CI (#12)
  • [x] PyPI wheels: installed into the top layer as pip and uv install them, checked against pixi install (#17)

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• [ ] Push. pixi oci push sends the image to any registry, with docker-style credentials. (#13)
  • [ ] pixi oci run. Rootless containers on Linux through unprivileged user namespaces, with no Docker, Podman or root, so CI runs the built image as a normal user. (#14)
Windows laptop (no admin, no VM) macOS Linux CI on Linux build yes yes yes yes validate, inspect yes yes yes yes check yes yes yes yes run no: needs a Linux kernel no: needs a Linux kernel where user namespaces are allowed yes

docs.title: After that
docs.text:
• [ ] pixi oci diff: two images compared layer by layer, with the packages behind each change and what a rebuild re-uploads (#26)
  • [ ] An examples/ directory of real pixi workspaces, small to a few hundred packages, planned in CI and measured (#22)
  • [ ] Multi-platform image indexes: linux-64 and linux-aarch64 under one tag (#15)
  • [ ] pixi's activation variables, and an entrypoint from a pixi task (#16)
  • [ ] Private channels, with pixi's own credentials (#18)
  • [ ] A pixi-sbom SBOM attached to the image, and pixi-policy as a gate before pushing (#19)
  • [ ] A release, and a package on conda-forge: pixi global install pixi-oci (#20)

docs.title: Related projects
docs.text:
• conda-docker built images from conda environments without Docker, and is this project's closest ancestor.
  • apko and ko do the same for Alpine packages and Go binaries; pixi-oci aims to be that for pixi.lock.
  • Pixitainer (pixi containerize) builds Apptainer, Singularity and Docker images through those tools.
  • prefix.dev's rattler-oci registry (in preview) builds images on the server when they are pulled.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Every error names what went wrong and, where there is one, what to do; this page has the rest. Messages are shown as pixi-oci prints them, with the variable parts in angle brackets.

docs.title: Choosing what to build
docs.text:
the lockfile has no environment named <name> : The help line lists the environments the lockfile has. Pick one with -e; without -e it is default.

environment <name> is not locked for <platform> : Add the platform to the workspace and lock again: pixi workspace platform add linux-64, then pixi lock. The help line lists the platforms that are locked.

<platform> is not a Linux platform, so no container image can be built for it : Images carry Linux programs. Pass a linux-* platform with -p: linux-64 for x86 servers, linux-aarch64 for ARM ones. Without -p, pixi-oci picks Linux on your machine's architecture, so this appears only when -p named osx-* or win-*.

environment <name> has PyPI packages that are not wheels: <names> : pixi-oci installs wheels and builds nothing. These were locked as an sdist, a git checkout or a local path. Lock a version that publishes wheels for the platform (most do), get the package from conda-forge instead, or build the wheel and depend on it.

<name>'s wheel holds <path>, which its RECORD ... : The wheel's files do not match the list of hashes inside it. The wheel matched the lockfile's hash, so it was published this way: report it to the package.

environment <name> builds <n> packages from source: <names> : pixi-oci installs built conda packages. Build those with pixi build, publish them to a channel, and lock the published packages.

<path> is not a lockfile pixi-oci can read : Either it is not a pixi.lock, or a newer pixi wrote it in a format this pixi-oci predates. Update pixi-oci.

could not read <path> : No lockfile there. Run pixi lock in the workspace, or pass --lockfile.

docs.title: Downloading
docs.text:
could not download <url> : The cause follows the message. Behind a proxy, set HTTPS_PROXY. A channel that needs credentials is not supported yet.

<name> downloaded from <url> does not match the lockfile's sha256 : The bytes the channel served are not the ones that were locked: the channel replaced the file, or something between you and it changed it. Nothing was cached or used. Lock again to take the channel's current file, but find out why it changed first.

the lockfile records no sha256 for <name>, so its download cannot be checked : A current pixi records one for every conda package. Lock again with it.

could not use the package cache at <path> : The cache directory is not writable, or the disk is full. Point --cache-dir (or PIXI_OCI_CACHE_DIR) somewhere else.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
<path> already exists : pixi-oci does not overwrite an image unless asked: add --force, or pick another --output.

the image prefix must be an absolute path, not <prefix> : --prefix is a Linux path inside the image, such as /opt/env.

<name> is a noarch Python package, but the environment has no python to install it for : The package needs a python in the same environment to know where site-packages is. Add python to the environment.

<name>'s location in the lockfile is not a URL, so it has no repodata record to install from : The package was locked from a local path. Publish it to a channel (a local one served over file:// works) and lock from there.

<name> would install <path>, which is outside the environment's prefix : The archive's paths.json names a path with .. or a root. A real conda package never does; treat the archive as damaged or crafted and check where it came from.

<name>'s paths.json lists <path>, but its archive has no such file and <name>'s archive has no readable <file> : The archive is damaged or was built by a tool that does not follow the conda package format. Rebuild or re-download it.

<name>'s archive holds <path> as a hard link, which pixi-oci cannot place yet : A tar hard link inside a package is rare and not supported yet. Please open an issue naming the package.

could not write <path> or could not write the layer : Usually a full disk; the cause follows the message. A build needs room for the layers, and while a .tar is assembled, the layers twice. A failed build leaves no .tar at the output path, and a layout directory without its index.json, so nothing half-written passes for an image.

docs.title: Running the image
docs.text:
exec /opt/env/bin/python: no such file or directory from docker run or podman run : The program exists; its loader does not: the image has no glibc. Build it on a base image with --base (Base images). pixi oci check reports this, on any OS, before you load the image.

... is not pinned to a digest : --base takes an image with its digest, so the build stays reproducible. crane digest <image> or skopeo inspect docker://<image> prints it (Base images).

... refused access to ... when pulling a base : The registry wants credentials. Log in with docker login or podman login (or set up a credential helper): pixi-oci reads what they store.

... has no image for linux/arm64/v8 : The base's index has no image for the platform being built. Pick a base built for it, or build for a platform the base has.

pixi oci check reports library: libX11.so.6 ..., or another library : A binary in the environment links to a library no package in the environment provides. conda-forge's tk, for one, links to libX11.so.6, so tkinter needs xorg-libx11 in the environment (pixi add xorg-libx11). If nothing in the image uses that binary, the image runs without it.

pixi oci is an unknown command : pixi cannot see the executable: see Installation.

docs.title: Still stuck
docs.text: Run with RUST_BACKTRACE=1 if it crashed, and open an issue with the command, the full output, pixi oci --version and, if you can share it, the lockfile.

docs.title: Building on Windows
docs.text:
pixi-oci builds Linux images on Windows with no admin rights, no WSL and no VM. It runs from PowerShell, cmd or Git Bash alike; the shell makes no difference.

pixi oci plan  -p linux-64
pixi oci build -p linux-64 --tag app:1.0 -o app.tar

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text:
A Linux layer holds things a Windows file system cannot: Unix file modes (which files are executable), symlinks (Windows needs admin rights or Developer Mode to make one), and names that differ only in case (NTFS treats Makefile and makefile as one file). pixi-oci never puts a layer's files on the host. It reads each package archive one entry at a time and writes the entry, with its mode, symlink target and exact name, straight into the layer's tar. The only files it writes on Windows are package archives, layer blobs and temporary files, all named by hashes.

Git Bash does not change any of this: it is a shell on the same Windows file system. It is fine to use, and so are PowerShell and cmd.

docs.title: The same image as Linux
docs.text: An image built on Windows is the same image, byte for byte, as one built from the same lockfile on Linux or macOS. CI builds a test image on all three on every change and fails if the digests differ. That is what lets you build on Windows and trust what CI tests on Linux.

docs.title: What needs a Linux machine
docs.text:
A Linux image's programs are Linux binaries, so running them needs a Linux kernel, which Windows only has inside WSL 2 or a VM. Without those:

On Windows pixi oci plan Yes pixi oci build, for linux-64 or linux-aarch64 Yes pixi oci validate Yes pixi oci inspect Yes pixi oci check: will it run? Yes: it reads the binaries and scripts, and runs nothing Other OCI tools (skopeo inspect, crane validate) Yes, with those tools installed Run the image No: it needs a Linux kernel. CI runs it for you.

pixi oci check tells you, on Windows, whether the image would run: a missing loader or library, a script whose interpreter is not there, an entrypoint not on PATH. A rootless pixi oci run for Linux and CI is on the roadmap.

docs.title: Paths
docs.text:
• Output: -o C:\work\app.tar or -o .\app.tar; either kind of slash works.
  • Cache: %LOCALAPPDATA%\pixi-oci by default; --cache-dir or PIXI_OCI_CACHE_DIR move it.
  • Inside the image everything is a Linux path: --prefix /opt/env, --workdir /work.

docs.title: Corporate networks
docs.text: Downloads honour HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY, and TLS is checked against the Windows certificate store, so a proxy whose certificate your IT department installed there works without extra settings. Channels that need credentials are not supported yet.

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text:
Report it privately through GitHub: Report a vulnerability (Security → Advisories → Report a vulnerability). The report is visible only to the maintainer until an advisory is published.

Please do not open a public issue for a security problem, and please do not disclose it elsewhere before a fix is out. If GitHub's form is not available to you, open a public issue asking for a private channel, with no details in it, and one will be arranged.

What to include: the version (pixi oci --version), the platform you built on, the command you ran, and the smallest lockfile or package that reproduces it. For anything involving a crafted archive, attach the archive. A crash needs a backtrace (RUST_BACKTRACE=1).

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
Acknowledgment Within 3 business days. This is a small project with one maintainer; if you have heard nothing after that, ping the advisory thread. Assessment Within 10 business days: whether it is in scope, how severe, and a rough fix timeline. Fix and disclosure A patch release, then a published GitHub Security Advisory with a CVE where one is warranted. Credit You are named in the advisory unless you would rather not be. Say which you prefer.

There is no bug bounty.

docs.title: Supported versions
docs.text: pixi-oci has not had a release yet. Until it does, fixes land on main; once releases start, the newest one is the supported one.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
pixi-oci reads input an attacker may control, and writes images other people will run, so both ends matter.

It reads:

  • Lockfiles: pixi.lock, YAML from a repository you may not have written.
  • Conda archives: .conda (zip and zstd) and .tar.bz2 (tar and bzip2), their info/ files and their content, downloaded from the channels the lockfile names or read from local paths.
  • HTTP responses from those channels. A response is untrusted even when the host is; every archive is checked against the sha256 the lockfile recorded before anything reads it.

In scope, from any of those:

  • A file written on the build host outside the output, cache and temporary directories. A build is designed to write nothing on the host from an archive's member names: layers are written from the archive's entries straight into the layer's tar.
  • A file placed in the image outside the environment's prefix by a package's paths, or an archive whose content differs from what the lockfile's sha256 covers and is used anyway.
  • A panic, a hang, or an allocation that grows with an attacker's input past --max-memory's design, such as a decompression bomb that exhausts memory or disk.
  • An image that is not what the lockfile describes in a way an attacker can arrange on purpose: a package silently dropped, swapped, or given different bytes.
  • A network request to a host the lockfile does not name, or a credential sent to a host that should not see it.

Out of scope:

  • Vulnerabilities in the packages you put in an image. pixi-oci builds what the lockfile locks; scanning it is the job of a scanner (and of pixi-sbom).
  • Anything that needs an attacker who can already write to the build machine, the cache or the output directory.
